sentences: Bigger brains might hold more concepts as pockets of reducibility, but how much more remains genuinely unclear.
That capacity for concepts rests on mundane shared mechanics: sensory input compressed through layers into one decision stream.
Language's discreteness and single-threaded grammar emerge from this mechanics, and bigger brains would shift that balance, not escape it.
The same balance holds beyond language: sensing and acting gain more features with scale, still bounded by irreducibility.
Tracing concepts through perception and language, abstraction appears as a historical tower of such pockets, reaching toward the ruliad's limit.
Computational language stress-tests that tower, showing how far brains can routinize abstraction before hitting pure irreducibility.
Since one brain sustains only a single thread of thought, scaling beyond it means coordinating many threads through society instead.
These threads converge: a bigger mind is simply a larger region of the ruliad, mind-like only while bounded and single-threaded.
Machine consciousness is still unsettled, yet it already bears on rights, ethics, and how we see ourselves.
Before any evidence is weighed, built-in biases already tilt us toward seeing minds in machines.
Stripped of bias, the real question becomes whether computation itself can ever be enough for experience.
Computation alone looks insufficient, so action must proceed under genuine uncertainty about what's inside any machine.
Unable to resolve the question outright, the stakes return to what kind of beings we choose to remain.
GPT-3's scale-up succeeds where architecture tweaks alone would not, reviving a long-dismissed idea about intelligence.
Beyond GPT-3, scale's benefits recur everywhere, but why size itself breeds intelligence remains unexplained.
Scale's general power now gets a concrete mechanism: predicting text may force models toward real understanding.
Why scale works is argued; whether anyone will wager enough compute on it is another matter.
That lone bet now looks vindicated by hindsight, yet most experts still haven't revised their skepticism.
Vindicated or not, scale carries a side effect: models trained on human data start acting like agents.
Even stripped of human data, agency may still emerge from any system complex enough to require inferring rules.
The case for scale-born intelligence and agency rests here, unresolved beyond pointers to further reading.
A single corroded find raises a core claim still unsettled: who built this first known computer, and when.
Before any mechanism can be explained, its scattered physical remains must first be sorted and identified.
With the gears catalogued, attention turns to what the front face actually displayed and how reliably.
Granted a calendar and sun-moon pointers, the question becomes what else those dials could track.
The front having handled sun and moon, the back dials extend reach to decades-long eclipse and calendar cycles.
All five back dials now accounted for, one stray gear reopens the question of undiscovered planetary works.
Unable to settle planets from evidence alone, rival teams built competing gear schemes to test the idea.
Granting the device was imprecise and likely not unique, its lineage is sought in later geared instruments abroad.
Debate over its original design settled or not, the mechanism's afterlife continues in museums and popular culture.
A scientist opens by promising to explain how to avoid fooling ourselves, without yet saying how.
Popular beliefs keep failing simple tests, setting up the need for a name for this failure.
That failure gets a name, Cargo Cult Science, and its missing ingredient: strict honesty with oneself.
That honesty now extends outward, from guarding against self-deception to leveling with the public and policymakers.
Concrete cases show integrity routinely abandoned under pressure, closing with a wish rather than a fix.
